lesson.title: dy: The Change the Tangent Line Predicts
lesson.summary: The differential dy = f'(x) dx is the change in y that the tangent line predicts for a given step dx, a close but not exact stand-in for the true change in y.
lesson.body:
The actual change in a function is written Delta y = f(x + Delta x) - f(x): start somewhere, take a step, see how much the output moved. The differential dy is a different, related quantity: dy = f'(x) dx. It is the change you would get if you moved along the tangent line instead of the actual curve, which makes it exactly the y-step produced by the linearization formula from two chapters back, just written in a new notation.

Because dy = f'(x) dx, it depends on two things: where you are, through f'(x), and how big a step you take, through dx. It is best read as a prediction rather than a measurement. Delta y tells you what actually happened to the curve; dy tells you what the tangent line said would happen. Keeping the two symbols distinct matters, because they usually are not exactly equal.

Consider y = x^2 at x = 3, with a step of dx = 0.1. Since f'(x) = 2x, dy = f'(3)(0.1) = 6(0.1) = 0.6. Now compare that with the true change: Delta y = f(3.1) - f(3) = 9.61 - 9 = 0.61. The predicted change dy = 0.6 is very close to the actual change 0.61, off by only one hundredth, which is the differential doing exactly what it promises: a fast, nearly accurate stand-in for Delta y.

That gives a second way to write the linearization formula. Since f(x + dx) is approximately f(x) + dy, and dy = f'(x) dx, this is the same statement as L(x + dx) = f(x) + f'(x) dx from the linearization chapter, just phrased in the language of differentials instead of tangent lines.
